title: Six orders
hook: the Mishnah has six orders; Shas is their abbreviation

segments.voice: Yesterday, the amora, Resh Lakish and his objections, and your line: the explainers. Did anyone give you an objection worth having? Today, the map of everything they explained. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

On a shelf in a house of study stands a long row of matching volumes, tall and heavy, with gold letters on the spines. Someone points at the whole row and calls it by one short word: Shas. You hear it in other places too. A person who knows Shas. A celebration for finishing Shas. It sounds like a nickname, and in a way it is. It's two Hebrew letters, shin and samekh, standing in for two words. And those two words are a map of the whole Mishnah.
screen: `A LONG ROW OF HEAVY VOLUMES.` → `ONE SHORT WORD: SHAS.` → `TWO LETTERS, TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Shas. Shin for shishah, six. Samekh for sedarim, orders. Six orders. The Mishnah, and the Talmud built on it, is arranged in six large sections, and Shas became a name for the whole thing. Here they are. Zeraim, seeds: blessings and farming. Moed, appointed time: Shabbat, festivals and fasts. Nashim, women: marriage, divorce and vows. Nezikin, damages: courts, property, harm, and the sayings of the fathers. Kodashim, holy things: the Temple's offerings. Tohorot, purities: what makes a person or a thing pure or impure. Students have a traditional way to hold the list: take the first letter of each name and you get two little Hebrew words, z'man nakat, roughly, he took time. Zeraim, Moed, Nashim. Nezikin, Kodashim, Tohorot. Now listen to the list as a whole. It starts in a field, with food. Then it moves to the calendar, to the weeks and the seasons. Then into the home, between two people. Then out to the neighbors, the market and the court. Then up to the Temple. And finally to the body, the house, and what is pure. Some readers hear it as a map of a whole life: what you eat, when you rest, whom you love, how you treat the person next door, how you come near to God. Nothing is left out as too ordinary. A wedding and a pothole and a holy day all sit on the same shelf, under one short word. That's the claim hidden in the abbreviation: it all belongs to one Torah.
screen: `SHIN, SAMEKH: SHISHAH SEDARIM.` · `SEEDS, TIME, WOMEN.` · `DAMAGES, HOLY THINGS, PURITIES.` · `A FIELD, A CALENDAR, A HOME, A COURT.` · then, large: `SIX ORDERS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: say the six names. Sit, breathe, and on each out-breath say one name quietly. Zeraim. Moed. Nashim. Nezikin. Kodashim. Tohorot. Go round again, slower. This time, with each name, let one part of your own life come to mind. A meal for seeds. Your calendar for time. Someone you love for women and marriage. A neighbor for damages. A quiet moment for holy things. Your own body for purities. Keep going round until the bell ends. The bell holds the time.
Shas. Short for shishah sedarim, the six orders of the Mishnah, and a name for the whole Talmud built on them. Today's word.

Your line: six orders. Today, notice when your day moves from one of them to another: from a meal, to a calendar, to a person, to a neighbor. Tomorrow, the first order, seeds. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Students learn the six orders by name, and when a person or a study group completes a tractate or the whole of Shas, they hold a siyum, a festive meal, and recite the hadran, which promises to return to what was learned.
